claims.claim: Dirda says the narrator conveys the real story behind the legends of the Archmage Ged.
claims.source: Michael Dirda, NEA Big Read teacher's guide to A Wizard of Earthsea (2008)
claims.quote: the real story behind the legends of the Archmage Ged

claims.claim: Plotz says Le Guin trains a spotlight on all the things that we make up and then treat as real.
claims.source: John Plotz, Ursula Le Guin's Earthsea (2023), p. 34, quoted in Stephanie Burt, Strange Horizons, 6 November 2023
claims.quote: trains a spotlight on all the things that we make up
claims.page: p. 34, as quoted in the review

claims.claim: Burt says Le Guin invites the reader in and holds the reader back.
claims.source: Stephanie Burt, review of Plotz, Strange Horizons, 6 November 2023
claims.quote: invites us in and holds us back

claims.claim: Le Guin says she drew a map of islands she knew nothing about and named them happily.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 2015 interview with John Plotz, transcribed in Public Books, 21 February 2024
claims.page: interview transcript, on drawing the Earthsea map

claims.claim: Le Guin grants that the archaic manner is a perfect distancer but says it must be done perfectly.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: The archaic manner is indeed a perfect distancer

claims.claim: Le Guin names ichor as the infallible touchstone of the seventh-rate among fantasy's fancy words.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: the infallible touchstone of the seventh-rate: Ichor

claims.claim: Le Guin concludes that archaisms are not essential to fantasy.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: After all, archaisms are not essential.

claims.claim: Le Guin praises Eddison's archaic prose as exact, clear and powerful despite or because of its archaisms.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)

claims.claim: Le Guin criticises Leiber and Zelazny for alternating a colloquial American style with old formal usages within one work.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)

claims.claim: Le Guin says realistic detail is used in fantasy only in lesser matters, to ground the story and prevent an overload of the improbable.
claims.quote: Only in lesser matters is realistic detail used to ground the story

claims.claim: Le Guin says that with the most ordinary ingredients, naming everyday language among them, and care and skill in using them, a writer can make something extremely good.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Navigation Q1: How do you make something good?", Book View Cafe, 27 July 2015 (text at ursulakleguin.com)

claims.claim: Le Guin says pity and terror are achieved more often through brevity, a few telling details and a great deal left unsaid than through wallowing in a bloodbath.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Navigating the Ocean of Story: Session 2, Round 1", Book View Cafe, 2016
claims.quote: brevity, a few telling details, a great left unsaid
claims.page: answer to Lauren, question 5 (the page as fetched reads "a great left unsaid")

claims.claim: Le Guin praises a Patrick O'Brian scene of a ship going down with five hundred men aboard as one that could not be shorter, more silent, or more shocking.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Navigating the Ocean of Story: Session 2, Round 1", Book View Cafe, 2016
claims.quote: could not be shorter, more silent, or more shocking

claims.claim: Le Guin advises describing just enough of a character's appearance to give the noticing reader a clear clue, saying one physical detail will often do it.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Navigating the Ocean of Story: Session 2, Round 1", Book View Cafe, 2016
claims.quote: Often one physical detail will do it

claims.claim: Le Guin says a reader will learn what an unexplained invented term means but may have to wait a while, and that lazy readers find waiting uncomfortable.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Navigating the Ocean of Story: Session 2 — Three New Questions", Book View Cafe, 21 March 2016
claims.quote: The reader will learn what it is
